entry: Philosophical problem articulated by [[David Hume]] concerning whether [[Morality|moral]] statements about what ought to be can be inferred from objective statements about what is. Hume distinguished descriptive statements from prescriptive ones and argued that it is not obvious how one can coherently move from the first to the second. In *A Treatise of Human Nature* (1739–40), he warned that the step from is to ought must be observed and explained. Hume's law, or Hume's guillotine, is the thesis that an ethical conclusion cannot be inferred from purely descriptive factual premises. G. E. Moore's open-question argument reaches a similar view and was aimed at ethical naturalists, who identify moral properties with natural ones. The problem is closely related to the fact–value distinction in [[Epistemology]], although that discussion may also encompass [[Aesthetics|aesthetics]]. Responses include non-cognitivist views such as emotivism, which treat "ought" statements as expressions of attitude, and John Searle's 1964 argument that institutional facts such as promises carry normative force. Consensus on a resolution remains elusive.

American writer and professor of biochemistry. Asimov is best known for hard [[Science fiction|science fiction]], and during his lifetime he was considered one of the "Big Three" science fiction writers, along with [[Robert A. Heinlein]] and [[Arthur C. Clarke]]. He wrote or edited more than 500 books. His best-known work is the Foundation series, about a fallen space empire; its first three books won a Hugo Award in 1966 for "Best All-Time Series." He wrote the Robot series, in which he introduced the Three Laws of Robotics in the short story "Runaround." His popular science books, such as *Asimov's Chronology of Science and Discovery*, explain concepts historically, and he also wrote on [[Chemistry]], [[Astronomy]], and [[Mathematics]]. He was president of the American Humanist Association. Several entities are named for him, including the asteroid (5020) Asimov, a crater on [[Mars]], and [[Honda|Honda's]] humanoid robot ASIMO.

Second Hebrew patriarch in [[Judaism]], son of [[Abraham]] and Sarah and father of [[Jacob]]. Isaac is an important figure in the [[Abrahamic religions]], including Samaritanism, Christianity, Islam, the Baháʼí Faith, and Rastafari. He first appears in the [[Torah]], and he is the grandfather of the twelve tribes of Israel. His name means "he will laugh," reflecting the laughter of Abraham and Sarah when they were told they would have a child in old age. He is the only patriarch whose name was never changed, and the only one who did not move out of [[Canaan]]. According to the narrative, he died aged 180. In the Akedah, or Binding of Isaac, God tests Abraham by ordering him to sacrifice Isaac on Mount Moriah; an [[Angel|angel]] stops him at the last moment, and a ram is sacrificed instead. Isaac married Rebekah, and their sons were Esau and Jacob.

Queen of Castile and León (r. 1474–1504), known with her husband as the Catholic Monarchs. Her marriage to [[Ferdinand II of Aragon|Ferdinand]] in 1469 created the basis for the de facto unification of Spain, and with his help she won the War of the Castilian Succession and secured her position as queen. She reorganized the government, brought the crime rate down, and cleared the debt left by her half-brother, King Henry IV. Her reign marked the end of the [[Reconquista]] and the start of the [[Spanish Empire]]. Other actions included the Alhambra Decree, which ordered the mass expulsion of Jews from Spain; initiating the [[Spanish Inquisition]]; and financing the 1492 voyage of [[Christopher Columbus]] to the [[New World]]. [[Pope Alexander VI]] granted the couple the title "Catholic Monarch." Her beatification process opened in 1958, and in 1974 she was granted the title Servant of God.

French actress and singer known for tragic, emotionally complex characters, particularly in psychological films. She has won a record five César Awards for Best Actress, for *Possession* (1981), *One Deadly Summer* (1983), *Camille Claudel* (1988), *La Reine Margot* (1994), and *La Journée de la jupe* (2009). She was nominated for the [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] for Best Actress at age 20 for *The Story of Adèle H.* (1975), becoming the youngest nominee in the category at the time, and again for *Camille Claudel*. She also won the Best Actress Award at the [[Cannes Film Festival]] for *Possession* and *Quartet* (1981).

American-born dancer and choreographer, a pioneer of [[Modern dance|modern dance]]. Born and raised in California, she lived and danced in Western Europe, the United States, and Soviet Russia from the age of 22. Her natural, free movement contrasted with the rigidity of [[Ballet|ballet]], and she drew inspiration from Greek vase paintings and bas-reliefs in the [[British Museum]]. After working in Augustin Daly's company in [[New York City]], she grew disillusioned with the form and moved to London in 1898, performing in the drawing rooms of the wealthy. In 1902 Loie Fuller invited her to tour Europe. Despite mixed reactions from critics, she inspired visual artists, including [[Auguste Rodin]], to create works based on her. In 1910 she met the occultist [[Aleister Crowley]] at a party. She died in [[Nice]], France, when her scarf became entangled in the wheel and axle of the car in which she was traveling.

Israelite prophet of the 8th century BC, after whom the Book of Isaiah in the [[Hebrew Bible]] is named. The name means "[[Yahweh]] is salvation." He probably began his ministry in the 740s BC and prophesied during the reigns of the kings of Judah Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. When Hezekiah rebelled against Assyria and allied with the king of [[Egypt]], Sennacherib invaded Judah, and a detachment threatened [[Jerusalem]]; Isaiah urged Hezekiah to resist. According to 2 Kings 19, an angel of God slew 185,000 Assyrian men in one night. The traditional view holds that one man wrote all 66 chapters of the book, possibly in two periods between 740 BC and c. 686 BC. A widely held alternative attributes parts of chapters 1–39 to the prophet and dates the rest to the exile in Babylon in the 6th century BC, when the later chapters may be the work of a school of prophets.

British social and political theorist, philosopher, and historian of ideas. Born in [[Riga]] to a Russian-Jewish family, he was fluent in [[Yiddish]], Russian, German, French, and English, and as a child he witnessed the [[Russian Revolution]] in Petrograd. His family moved to England in 1921, and he was educated at St Paul's School and Corpus Christi College, Oxford. He was elected to a prize fellowship at All Souls College in 1932. From 1957 to 1967 he was Chichele Professor of Social and Political Theory at the [[University of Oxford]], and in 1966 he helped create Wolfson College. He translated works by [[Ivan Turgenev]] into English, was knighted in 1957, and served as president of the British Academy from 1974 to 1978. Berlin's work on liberal theory and value pluralism, and his opposition to [[Marxism]] and [[Communism]], has had a lasting influence.

English civil and marine engineer, considered one of the greatest figures of the [[Industrial Revolution]]. As the first engineer of the Great Western Railway, he designed its London–[[Bristol]] main line and built the Box Tunnel, the longest in the world at the time. His steamships, the SS Great Western, SS Great Britain, and SS Great Eastern, were the largest of their time. The SS Great Britain was the first iron-hulled, propeller-driven ship to make a transatlantic crossing. His career was marred by financial and engineering setbacks, and his broad gauge became greatly problematic for the railway in the long term. The Thames Tunnel was completed only after his involvement ended, and the Clifton Suspension Bridge was completed after his death. Brunel died shortly after the SS Great Eastern suffered a huge explosion on her maiden voyage. In 2002 he was placed second in a [[BBC]] poll of the "100 Greatest Britons."

City in central Iran and capital of Isfahan Province, 440 kilometers south of [[Tehran]]. With a population of approximately 2,238,000, it is Iran's third-most populous city after Tehran and [[Mashhad]], and it has the second-largest metropolitan area. The city lies at the intersection of Iran's two principal routes, north–south and east–west. It flourished between the 9th and 18th centuries. Under the [[Safavid dynasty]] it became the capital of Iran for the second time in its history, under [[Abbas the Great]], and it is known for its Persian–Muslim architecture, grand boulevards, covered bridges, palaces, and tiled mosques. Naqsh-e Jahan Square is one of the largest city squares in the world and a [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]]. Its fame led to the Persian proverb "Isfahan is half the world." The region was settled as early as the Paleolithic period, and under [[Cyrus the Great]] the religiously diverse city became an early example of royal religious tolerance.

Figure in the Abrahamic religions, the first son of [[Abraham]] and Hagar, the handmaiden of Abraham's wife Sarah. In the [[Book of Genesis]], Sarah, who had been barren, offered Hagar to Abraham, and Ishmael was born when Abraham was 86. After [[Isaac]] was born, Sarah asked that Hagar and Ishmael be sent away, and Abraham agreed only after God promised that Ishmael would become a great nation. According to the Genesis narrative, Ishmael died at the age of 137. In [[Islam]], he is regarded as a prophet and the ancestor of the Ishmaelites and patriarch of Qaydār. Islamic tradition credits him, alongside Abraham, with building the [[Kaaba]] in [[Mecca]].

Mathematical model of [[Ferromagnetism|ferromagnetism]] in [[Statistical mechanics|statistical mechanics]], named after the physicists Ernst Ising and Wilhelm Lenz. Its discrete variables represent the magnetic dipole moments of atomic spins, each in one of two states, +1 or −1, that interact with neighboring spins on a lattice. The two-dimensional square-lattice version is one of the simplest statistical models to show a [[Phase transition|phase transition]]. Lenz proposed the model in 1920 and gave it to Ising as a problem. Ising solved the one-dimensional case, which has no phase transition. Lars Onsager gave an analytic solution of the two-dimensional model in 1944.

Major goddess in [[Ancient Egyptian religion|ancient Egyptian religion]] whose worship spread throughout the Greco-Roman world. In the myth of [[Osiris]], she resurrects her slain brother and husband, Osiris, and produces and protects his heir, [[Horus]]. She was believed to help the dead enter the afterlife and was considered the divine mother of the pharaoh, who was likened to Horus. During the New Kingdom she took on traits of [[Hathor]] and was portrayed wearing Hathor's headdress. In the first millennium BCE, Osiris and Isis became the most widely worshipped Egyptian deities. In the [[Hellenistic period]], Greeks and Egyptians worshipped her alongside the new god Serapis, and her cult became part of Roman religion. Her worship ended with the rise of [[Christianity]] in the fourth through sixth centuries CE. She continues to appear in [[Modern paganism|modern paganism]] and esotericism, often as a personification of nature.

Twelfth sultan of [[Aceh]] (r. 1607–36), under whom the sultanate reached its greatest territorial extent and became the strongest power and wealthiest state in the western [[Indonesia|Indonesian]] archipelago and the [[Strait of Malacca]]. The name means "young Alexander," and his conquests were often compared to those of [[Alexander the Great]]. Aceh became an international center of [[Islam|Islamic]] learning and trade. His navy of heavy [[Galley|galleys]] took Deli in 1612, Aru and Johor in 1613, and Pahang in 1617, and his strength threatened the Portuguese holding of Malacca. In 1629 he sent several hundred ships against Malacca; according to Portuguese sources, all of them were destroyed along with 19,000 men. His rule was also marked by the execution of family members and officials suspected of disloyalty. His death in 1636 ended the founding House of Meukuta Alam, and the sultanate entered a period of decline.

Capital city of [[Pakistan]], planned in the 1960s and established in 1967 along the Margalla Hills. It replaced [[Karachi]] as the national capital, and its name means "City of [[Islam]]." The city is the country's tenth-most populous, with a population of over 1.1 million, and is federally administered as part of the Islamabad Capital Territory. It lies north of [[Rawalpindi]], and the two form a metropolitan area of over 5.7 million inhabitants. The Greek architect Constantinos Apostolou Doxiadis developed its master plan, dividing the city into eight zones. It is home to more than twenty universities and the country's flagship Faisal Mosque, and as of 2025 its HDI of 0.924 is the highest of any district in Pakistan.

Multi-service military force of [[Iran]], established by [[Ruhollah Khomeini]] in May 1979 after the [[Iranian Revolution]]. It has five branches: Ground Forces, Aerospace Force, Navy, Quds Force, and Basij. Its constitutional mandate is to ensure the integrity of the Islamic Republic, which most interpretations take to include preventing foreign interference and thwarting coups. The Quds Force arms and advises pro-Iranian groups abroad, such as [[Hezbollah]] and [[Hamas]]. With approximately 125,000 personnel as of 2024, the force has taken a growing role in Iranian politics and economics, and several governments, including the [[United States]], designate it a terrorist organization.

Transnational Salafi jihadist militant organization and internationally unrecognized quasi-state, also known as ISIL or ISIS. It held significant territory in [[Syria]] during the [[Syrian civil war]] and in [[Iraq]]. In 2014 it proclaimed a worldwide [[Caliphate|caliphate]] and claimed religious and political authority over all [[Muslims]], a claim not accepted by the vast majority of them. The [[United Nations]] designates it as a terrorist organization. At the end of 2015 its self-declared caliphate ruled an area with about 12 million people. By 2019 it had lost its last territories in West Asia, though affiliates retain significant territory in Africa. The group committed genocides against Yazidis and Iraqi Turkmen and carried out attacks outside its territory, including the [[November 2015 Paris attacks|November 2015 Paris attacks]].

Architectural styles of buildings associated with [[Islam|Islamic]] civilization, from the early history of the faith to the present. Early Islamic architecture drew on Roman, Byzantine, Iranian, and Mesopotamian traditions in the lands conquered during the early Muslim conquests. Later it developed distinctive minarets, muqarnas, and multifoil arches, and decorated surfaces with calligraphy, arabesques, and geometric motifs. Common building types include [[Mosque|mosques]], madrasas, tombs, palaces, hammams, and military [[Fortification|fortifications]]. The first mosque, built by [[Muhammad]] in [[Medina]] in 622, was a courtyard structure that became a model for early mosques elsewhere. Regional styles developed from local materials and dynasties, and the [[Taj Mahal]] is renowned for its white marble inlays. The style spans regions from the [[Iberian Peninsula]] to [[Southeast Asia]].

Visual art produced since the 7th century CE in territories inhabited or ruled by [[Muslims]]. Public Islamic art is traditionally non-representational, favoring plant forms, usually in spiraling arabesques, often combined with [[Calligraphy|calligraphy]] and geometric patterns in tiling on mosques and other buildings. Other forms include miniature painting, [[Glass|glass]], [[Pottery|pottery]], and textiles such as carpets and embroidery. Calligraphy holds a central place because the [[Quran]] is the written version of divine revelation. Early Islamic art was influenced by [[Roman art|Roman]], Early Christian (Byzantine), and Sassanian art, and later by Central Asian nomadic traditions and by [[Chinese art]]. Some interpretations of Islam ban depictions of living beings, a practice called aniconism, yet figurative painting flourished, especially in Persian, Mughal, and Ottoman miniatures. The term was first used by Western art historians in the late 19th century.

Lunar calendar of 12 months, of 354 or 355 days, used by most Muslims to date religious observances; it is also called the Hijri calendar. It dates from the Hijrah, the 622 CE migration of [[Muhammad]] from [[Mecca]] to [[Medina]], which established the first Muslim community. Its months govern the fast of [[Ramadan]] and the annual season of the [[Hajj]] pilgrimage. Because it has no intercalation, its dates move about 10 to 12 days earlier each Gregorian year and rotate through the seasons. In almost all countries where Islam is predominant, the civil calendar is the [[Gregorian calendar]]. It is the official calendar of [[Saudi Arabia]], often used alongside the Gregorian calendar for civil matters. It was established by the second caliph, [[Umar|Umar ibn al-Khattab]], in 637 or 638 CE.

Philosophy that emerges from the Islamic tradition, closely tied to the translation of Greek texts into Arabic. Early Islamic philosophy began with [[Al-Kindi]] in the 2nd century of the [[Islamic calendar|Islamic calendar]] (early 9th century CE) and declined with [[Averroes|Ibn Rushd]] in the 6th century of that calendar (late 12th century CE), broadly coinciding with the [[Islamic Golden Age]]. It drew on [[Aristotle]] and Neoplatonism, and its major figures included [[Al-Farabi]] and [[Avicenna|Ibn Sina]]. Philosophy persisted longer in the east of the Islamic world, in Safavid Iran, the Ottoman Empire, and the Mughal Empire, where schools such as Avicennism and Illuminationism flourished. [[Ibn Khaldun]] made important contributions to the philosophy of history in his *Muqaddimah*. Interest revived during the Nahda ("Awakening") movement in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

Divisions within [[Islam]] comprising sects, schools of jurisprudence, and schools of theology. The original schism among Kharijites, Sunnis, and Shias concerned succession after the death of the Prophet [[Muhammad]], and the largest division today is between [[Sunni Islam|Sunni]] and [[Shia Islam|Shia]] Muslims, of whom Sunnis make up 87–90%. Sunni Islam has four main schools of jurisprudence, Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, and Hanbali, and theological schools including Ash'ari, Maturidi, and Athari. Shia Islam is divided into Twelvers, who make up about 85% of Shias by a 2012 estimate, Ismailis, and Zaydis. The Ibadis are the only surviving branch of the Kharijites. [[Sufism]], a mystical orientation, cuts across both Sunni and Shia contexts, and Sunnis frequently regard groups such as the [[Ahmadiyya]] as deviant. Muslims who do not identify with any identifiable school are known as non-denominational Muslims.

Range of religious and political movements holding that [[Islam]] should influence political systems; their proponents hold that an Islamic political system is superior to [[Communism]], liberal democracy, and capitalism. Advocates emphasize the implementation of [[Sharia]], pan-Islamic political unity, and the creation of Islamic states. Prominent 20th-century figures include Rashid Rida, Hassan al-Banna, founder of the [[Muslim Brotherhood]], [[Sayyid Qutb]], Abul A'la Maududi, and [[Ruhollah Khomeini]], founder of the Islamic Republic of Iran. Groups include the Muslim Brotherhood, Turkey's Justice and Development Party, and [[Hamas]]. After the [[Arab Spring]], some post-Islamist currents became involved in democratic politics, while others formed militias such as the Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant. Islamists themselves prefer terms such as "Islamic movement," and critics say the term may encourage Islamophobia and stereotyping.

In [[Nuclear physics|nuclear physics]], a predicted set of superheavy isotopes that may have considerably longer [[Half-life|half-lives]] than known isotopes of those elements. Its existence is attributed to stabilizing effects of predicted magic numbers of [[Proton|protons]] and [[Neutron|neutrons]]. It is generally thought to center near copernicium and flerovium isotopes near the closed neutron shell at N = 184. Estimates of half-lives range from minutes or days to, in optimistic proposals, millions of years. No such nuclides have been found in nature, and scientists have not yet found a reaction that reaches its center. The synthesis of elements up to [[Oganesson|oganesson]] (Z = 118), with up to 177 neutrons, shows a slight stabilizing effect around elements 110 to 114.

Self-governing British Crown Dependency in the [[Irish Sea]], between [[Great Britain]] and [[Ireland]]. [[Charles III]] holds the title Lord of Mann as head of state and is represented by a Lieutenant Governor, while the United Kingdom handles defense and represents the island abroad. Irish missionaries following Saint Patrick spread [[Christianity]] there. The island passed through Norwegian and Scottish rule before coming under the feudal lordship of the English Crown in 1399. Its parliament, Tynwald, became in 1881 the first national legislative body to give women the right to vote in a general election, though this excluded married women. The economy relies on low taxes and offshore banking, and insurance and online gambling each generate 17% of GNI. The island is known for the TT (Tourist Trophy) motorcycle races and the tailless [[Manx cat]], and [[UNESCO]] awarded it biosphere reserve status in 2016.
